channel.title: Daily Byte
channel.description: Production systems under tight constraints run through this edition: tokenizer costs, push-path classifier budgets, isolation correctness, and consumer-hardware MoE inference.

item.title: Claude Haiku 5.5
item.description: Real pricing structure, hidden tokenizer cost increase, and reasoning-mode latency characteristics for production API budgeting. Claude Haiku 5.5 prices at $0.10/$0.50 per million tokens up to 100K, jumping 5x above that threshold. A new tokenizer inflates token counts by ~1.25x versus Haiku 4.5, an effective price hike. Reasoning cannot be disabled, defaults to medium, and max effort on a simple SVG took over 5 minutes. Takeaway: Compare total cost including tokenizer changes and reasoning overhead, not just list prices, before switching workloads to Haiku 5.5.

item.title: Secret protection must scale with software
item.description: GitHub's fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier blocks unstructured secrets in under 2ms on the push path, more than doubling prevention. One in three pull requests now involves an AI agent, and secrets appear in public code every two seconds. Mean time to manually revoke a leaked credential hovers around 40 days. GitHub's new fine-tuned ModernBERT classifier evaluates candidate secrets in context in under 2ms, potentially more than doubling push-time blocks. The piece frames secret protection as a coupled constraint problem of precision, latency, throughput, and cost. Takeaway: Pushing ML onto a developer's critical path is a coupled constraint problem: precision, latency, throughput, and cost must all be solved together.

item.title: Mechanizing Transactional Anomalous Patterns for Weak Isolation Levels
item.description: Isolation level definitions are foundational to database correctness, and this work mechanically verifies them while catching real gaps. Machine-checked formalization of weak database isolation level definitions using the Rocq proof assistant, applied to TAP-based isolation checking. The process exposed two flaws in the original pen-and-paper proofs: an underspecified transaction history model and a missed Read Atomicity violation. Fixes integrated into the Plume isolation checker. Takeaway: Pen-and-paper proofs of database isolation semantics are fallible; machine-checked verification caught gaps in a real isolation checker.

item.title: Cascadia: Resident 975B MoE Inference on Eleven AI PCs
item.description: Demonstrates splitting a 975B sparse model across 11 consumer PCs with measured throughput, latency, and long-context behavior. Eleven consumer Intel AI PCs, each holding six decoder layers in 64GB of RAM, jointly serve a 975B-parameter sparse model over gigabit ethernet using a custom OpenVINO runtime. Peak aggregate decode reaches 60.3 tokens/s at 88 concurrent streams; median first-token latency is 6.05s at 15 streams, and prompts up to 64k tokens still recover embedded code. Takeaway: Sparse-expert weights can be sharded across commodity PCs on gigabit ethernet, but first-token time scales quadratically with prompt length.
item.source: Tate Berenbaum (Not Community Labs Inc.) et al.

item.title: Docker Agent
item.description: It packages LLM agents as OCI artifacts and runs them through the Docker CLI, reusing container distribution for AI tooling. docker-agent is a Docker CLI plugin that runs AI agents defined declaratively in YAML, with MCP tool integration, multi-agent delegation, built-in RAG, and reasoning tools. Agents are packaged and distributed through any OCI registry. It supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, and local models via Docker Model Runner. Takeaway: Treating agent configurations as versioned, OCI-distributed YAML is a practical way to ship and share LLM workflows.

item.title: Rust Port of TypeScript (Tsc)
item.description: An LLM ported a production compiler from Go to Rust in two weeks for ~$24k, beating the Go version on real projects. Using Opus 5.5, the author ported Microsoft's TypeScript compiler from Go to Rust over about two weeks for roughly $24,000 in API spend. The Rust port passes all 181,711 Go baseline tests, matches the Go output on 120 open-source repositories, and type-checks real projects about 1.6x faster than the Go compiler on a geometric mean across six apps. Takeaway: A frontier LLM can port a large production compiler between languages in weeks for tens of thousands of dollars.

item.title: When Submarine Cables Go Dark: Understanding and Preparing for the Risks of Taiwan's International Internet Disconnection
item.description: A reproducible method shows 88 percent of Taiwan's popular websites have hidden foreign or multinational-cloud dependencies that would break under cable outages. Analysis of 2,179 Taiwan websites found 39.3 percent are foreign-dependent and 49.6 percent rely on local nodes of multinational public clouds or CDNs. Taiwan's 14 international cables face damage 5.1 times yearly versus a global average of 0.1 to 0.2, with international cable repairs averaging 32 days. Satellites offer only Gbps-class backup, three orders of magnitude below cable capacity. Commenters are uniformly positive about the paper's relevance, with one highlighting the smc.peering.tw cable map as a useful companion resource; no substantive disagreement emerges. Takeaway: Treat application-layer resource dependencies as a measurable graph; physical link health does not equal service reachability.

item.title: Janet on x32: 32-bit Pointers, 64-bit Speed, 25% Less RAM
item.description: x32 trades 4GB address space for ~25% RAM reduction and better cache use, but distro support is eroding. Janet compiled with the Linux x32 ABI uses 32-bit pointers on 64-bit hardware, cutting memory use by 13-46% in benchmarks. Tests showed near-identical speed once proper -mx32 flags are used; the -m32 fallback halves register count and slows programs 50%. Building requires patching Janet's value-layout headers and disabling FFI, and distros like Arch lack x32-enabled kernels entirely. Zig 0.17 ships x32 support as a fun exercise, while CHERI analysis suggests under 20% of pages hold pointers so savings are workload-dependent, and LWN reports x32 is now proposed for removal as 32-bit address space strains modern apps. Takeaway: x32 trades 4GB of address space for denser pointer-heavy heaps; the real obstacle is distro support, not performance.
